newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Rival Serb leaders headed for showdown in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Rival Serb leaders headed for showdown in Bosnia.

text.p: Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic and government opponents were set on a collision course on Friday as hardliners said they would ignore a presidential decision to dissolve the assembly.

The government of Bosnia's Serb territory, covertly led by indicted war criminal and wartime leader Radovan Karadzic, dismissed the president's move as unconstitutional and prepared to go ahead with the assembly session on Friday.
Deputies in Karadzic's ruling party arrived at a hotel in the mountains above Sarajevo for the session which was called to launch the removal of Plavsic as president.

On the eve of the assembly, government hardliners shut down the official television station in the northern town of Banja Luka, the power base for President Plavsic who has accused the ruling party of growing rich off war profiteering.
Plavsic raised the stakes on Thursday in her power struggle with Karadzic when she ordered the dissolution of the Bosnian Serb assembly and set new elections for September 1.
Policemen and army soldiers who have sided with Plavsic were guarding her offices in Banja Luka, where resentment runs high against the ruling party based in Pale, outside Saraejvo.
The former biology professor was a loyal deputy to Karadzic during Bosnia's 1992-95 war but she has blown the whistle on high level corruption since she was elected last year.
Plavsic has also urged cooperation with Western peacemaking to avoid further isolation and poverty for Bosnian Serb-controlled territory.
Karadzic annointed her as an obedient, fellow ultra-nationalist when he was forced to step down from office under heavy international pressure a year ago.
Twice indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, Karadzic has broken his promises to stay out of politics and continues to pull strings in the Serb republic.
Western governments were concerned that Karadzic -- who has actively obstructed the peace agreement -- might prevail in the confrontation, dealing a setback to peace efforts.
The Contact Group of major powers - - the United States, Britain, France, Germany and Russia -- lent tacit support to Plavsic and demanded Karadzic withdraw from the arena.

"The legal government bodies and institutions of the Republika Srpksa (Serb republic) must be respected. Radovan Karadzic, on the other hand, is indicted on war crimes and should be extradited," the Contact Group said in a statement.
Diplomats said the power struggle was a crucial test for the United States and European states struggling to salvage the shaky peace in Bosnia.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission said Plavsic deserved international support for showing a willingness to abide by the Dayton peace treaty.
"Now is the defining moment for the peace process," David Foley, a spokesman for the OSCE, told reporters.
The commander of the Bosnian Serb army, General Pero Colic, said the military would not take sides in the conflict but the general staff gave cautious backing to Plavsic this week.
The army lacks financial support and has been purged by Karadzic, who has poured money into a vast police force.
The long-running feud between Plavsic and Karadzic erupted last weekend when the president called for the suspension of the hardline interior minister, a staunch Karadzic loyalist.

British and U.S. soldiers in the NATO-led peace force set up checkpoints along roads in Serb-controlled territory and patrolled Banja Luka town to prevent possible violence from breaking out between Plavsic supporters and Karadzic's police.
"What we will not allow is for armed or violent actions to dictate how this political process will develop," NATO spokesman Major Chris Riley told reporters.
